paragraphs: Near the edge of a great forest, in a small and quiet cottage, lived a poor woodcutter, his wife, and their two children.
The boy was named Hansel. The girl was named Gretel.
They were kind and gentle children, but their days were not easy. Food was often scarce, and each winter felt longer than the one before.
One cold night, when the fire burned low, the children heard their parents speaking in worried voices.
“We have nothing left,” said the woman. “If we do not act, we will all starve.”
The woodcutter wept softly. “How can I leave my children in the forest?” he said.
But fear made their hearts heavy.
And a terrible plan was made.
Hansel lay awake beside his sister.
“Do not cry, Gretel,” he whispered. “I will find a way.”
When the house was silent, he slipped outside beneath the moonlight and filled his pockets with white pebbles that shone like silver in the dark.
Early the next morning, the family walked deep into the forest.
Hansel dropped the pebbles quietly behind him, one by one.
When they reached a quiet clearing, the parents lit a fire and told the children to wait.
Then… they walked away.
Hansel and Gretel waited.
When the moon rose, Hansel took his sister’s hand.
Together, they followed the shining pebbles through the night.
And by morning…
They were home again.
Their father wept with joy. But worry soon returned.
Food ran out once more.
And the cruel plan was made again.
This time, Hansel could not gather pebbles.
So as they walked into the forest, he crumbled bread in his pocket and dropped the crumbs along the path.
But when night came…
The birds had eaten every piece.
The trail was gone.
Hansel and Gretel walked through the forest.
All night. All the next day.
They were tired. They were hungry.
At last, they lay beneath a tree and slept.
On the third morning, they saw a little white bird singing sweetly.
They followed it through the trees…
And soon they came upon a wonderful sight.
A small house stood before them.
Its roof was made of bread. Its walls of cake. Its windows of clear sugar.
Hungry and amazed, they tasted the sweet walls.
A soft voice called out,
“Nibble, nibble, gnaw, Who is nibbling at my little house?”
An old woman appeared.
She smiled kindly and invited them in.
She gave them warm milk. Sweet cakes. Soft beds.
Hansel and Gretel thought they were safe.
But the woman was not kind.
She was a wicked witch who lured children with her candy house.
That very night, she laughed quietly.
“They will not escape me.”
In the morning, the witch locked Hansel in a cage and forced Gretel to work.
Each day she fed Hansel rich food… and gave Gretel nothing.
Each day she felt Hansel’s finger to see if he was growing fat.
But Hansel held out a little bone.
The witch, nearly blind, thought it was his finger.
And waited.
At last, she grew impatient.
“Tomorrow,” she said, “I will cook him.”
That morning, she ordered Gretel to heat the oven.
She planned to push the girl inside as well.
But Gretel was brave.
“I do not know how to look inside,” she said softly.
The witch bent over to show her.
And Gretel pushed.
The oven door closed.
The witch was gone.
Gretel ran to Hansel.
She opened his cage.
They hugged and cried and laughed all at once.
They were free.
Inside the house, they found chests of jewels.
They filled their pockets and hurried into the forest.
Soon they came to a wide river.
A gentle white duck swam near.
Gretel called softly.
The duck carried them across, one at a time.
At last, they saw their father’s cottage.
They ran to him.
They held him close.
Their stepmother was gone.
And with the jewels, hunger was gone too.
And so Hansel and Gretel…
Who once walked alone in fear…
Returned home in courage.
They learned something gentle and true.
That even in the darkest forest…
Love can light the way.
And kindness can always lead you home.
